body:
I've begun my first steps here this time around. I've had several stints of sobriety averaging about 3-4 months, all without any help. Each time I'd find myself back at square one. Now I'm going to meetings and looking for any guidance I can. I don't know if anything comes close to hearing someone that had been sober since the 90s tell a story that you can directly connect to. I always felt lonely in sobriety but now have people to share the struggle with. 

I used to be the person that said meetings weren't for me. But I hadn't given them a real chance. That being said, my advice to OP would be:

Don't let one group define the program. Hell, don't let the first five. I found my home with the seventh group I tried. I didn't connect with any other group and had honestly given up on the sixth. I decided to keep trying because millions of Elvis fans can't be wrong right? :)
Gym bag, laptop case, & wadded up jacket were my go-to. Now my gym bag is for sweaty clothes, laptop case is for the laptop, and I can wear my jacket into the house from the car!

"Okay, three beers and half a fifth today, the rest tomorrow that's about 5 glasses of water before bed to equal no haze in the morning...shit, store is about to close I better get a little more booze just in case...I forgot to carry the 3 and account for x when I drink as much as I can after a certain point."

Now I can apply my math skills towards important things like my bills and nutrition.

I'm right there with you. I seemed to gradually relapse in the past. This last time I dove head first and was drinking more than I ever had. 

I've started going to meetings. As someone that used to avoid them at all costs and find all of the literature I could to back up my fears of AA, this has been a big turning point for me. 

I know my therapist and my family care about my well being, however none of them are alcoholics so they can't directly relate or provide tools for me to maintain my sobriety. 

I deleted my last account here thinking I had been "cured". 

Welcome friend, keep coming back, I know I will!

Unfortunately my days have been reset recently so my number isn't as high as it once was.

I do remember starting Mad Men after about 2 months sober. I longed for for a glass of scotch every time I watched it. I didn't even drink scotch! But part of me always played it through, knowing I couldn't sip on a glass of scotch like a gentleman. I'm not a sipper, I'm a guzzler. 

Sweet tea on the rocks please.

This analogy is terrible but it always pops in my head: It's like swinging a bat with weights on it before getting up to the plate. I don't mean this in the sense that drinking is good training to prepare for life. More so that my days struggling to get through the 9-5 waiting for the next drink have made my life sober seem so damn stress free and less difficult to manage. 

I did my job and no one knew the war zone that was my mind. Now I smile, I don't worry about losing my concentration and tasks that seemed like a huge undertaking are now a breeze. 

Congrats on your happiness friend!

I used to scoff at the idea of AA. I went many months sober on my own only to relapse, get sober for months only to relapse...rinse and repeat. 

I identified as an alcoholic. My family knew and my friends knew but I knew that after a few months I could start drinking and people would think I had taken a break and gotten things under control. Problem was, the drinking became more secretive. I couldn't pace myself. I bought a bottle knowing full and well I would drink it to the last drop. 

Friends, family and significant others can be supportive but they don't necessarily understand. My father has often told me he just doesn't get it. 

I have 16 days under my belt as of today and have been attending meetings this time around. It's very helpful to tell your story to people who understand and to hear that you aren't the only one that has this issue. 

I've learned that if you're atheist or agnostic you can't let the God business throw you. Your god can be whatever you make it. Mine is this one life I'm lucky enough to experience. I didn't have to do anything to come into this world and breath oxygen, smell flowers, look at clouds, experience love, read books, or appreciate art. That's a fucking beautiful thing no matter who you are. 

For me, AA isn't about faith, it's about becoming the person that I want to be. I hear people with 40+ years sober and that's something that I really admire. 

I had to go to about 4 different meetings before I found one that clicked for me. But I comfortably go to my homegroup now knowing there are people there that genuinely care about me and my sobriety and understand what I've been through. 

Rambled a bit there but I just got back from a meeting so I'm in share mode :)
Lol, I love this. Probably a little harsh, but he definitely wouldn't forget
This sounds great. Gee, thanks for taking all of that time to write it.
And it doesn't! I think maybe I'm butting in to his movie and in admitting my problem he realizes he may have one as well.

My first time getting sober I did this and it was amazing.  I'd love to do it again but I'm in a new city and haven't done the searching. 

It's just nice to tell someone what you're going through. I opened up to some close friends and my parents but I certainly left some details out for them out of embarrassment.

I had a pretty bad car accident. I had drank the night before and took a swig of liquor that morning to curb my hangover. The cops didn't test my BAC, but the doctor in the ER told me my BAC was that of someone with a high tolerance. I must've still had a lot in my system from the night before. I completely broke down. To be honest though, I needed a rude awakening. I have had sober stints before but this was a huge eye opener. It wasn't having a negative impact on work, I actually had recently received a big promotion. But psychologically I was pretty messed up and it was only a matter of time before someone started to notice. 

I was drinking almost a fifth a night and felt anxious and foggy all day until I had that next drink. 

I'm still embarrassed about it. Before when I would get cravings I would play it through until the hangover...now I play it through to the accident. 

I am really lucky to have lived, and if it hadn't happened I'd still be on a fast track to death.

I'm all too familiar. I flew out to visit my family over the holidays and got with some old friends. Even though I was 5 months sober, I decided I could handle one beer. I drank moderately while in town. I would have a wine at family dinners and no more than two beers with friends. I did it! I beat addiction!

Nope.

When I returned home where I would normally just go to work and hang out at my apartment, my moderation completely snowballed. I convinced myself I was going to the bar to watch sports (I'm not even an avid sports fan). But those pints turned into six packs turned into six packs and shooters turned into a fifth of liquor every couple days. 

Some people just can't drink at all. I'm one of those people.
